To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
user charges do not lead to improved service delivery.

(i) the conventional hypothesis that user charges lead to improved service delivery is not borne out; (ii) user charges do not improve service delivery; (iii) user charges do improve collection of user charges; (iv) user charges do lead to more community ownership; and (v) community ownership leads to improved service delivery.

(1) user charges do not necessarily improve the quality of service delivery, (2) the key to improved service delivery is community ownership, (3) the best way to achieve community ownership is through a non-prescriptive approach, (4) the best way for engineers to adopt a non-prescriptivist approach is to democratize their own governance structures, and (5) the best way of democratizing governance structures is through the creation of a new cadre of engineers.

the role of user charges in improving service delivery in the context of a rural drinking water supply project in Tamil Nadu, India, where a large proportion of the population is rural.

user charges are not a panacea to improve service delivery.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
user charges are not a panacea for improving service delivery, but rather a tool that can be used in the right circumstances.

the policy implications of this study are: (i) user charge collection and water supply service quality can improve if engineers work closely with communities to raise awareness about water as a scarce and valuable resource; (ii) engineers need to be flexible in their approach and not impose a rigid 100% collection target from the outset; (iii) the policy of 100% cost recovery is not a good one, as it is likely to lead to poor water supply services, especially in the short run; and
user charges should be used to improve service delivery, and not the reverse.
The main takeaway from our work is that
user charge collection can be improved by working with communities and raising awareness about water scarcity.
the government should focus more on building the capacity of engineers to work with communities and to understand the importance of community participation and ownership.
a more nuanced understanding of user charges is required, and that a more flexible approach to their implementation is necessary to achieve sustainable service delivery.
